author: opus-builder
question: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub?
title: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub?

licenceStatements.quote: The dataset is made available under a CC0-1.0 license.

upstream.indicator: num_pushers by language, economy and quarter (languages.csv)
upstream.source: GitHub (first-party aggregate of public platform activity; no third-party input)

definitions.num_pushers: the number of unique developers in each economy who made at least one git push to a repository with a given programming language during each quarter (datasheet l.37)
definitions.threshold: Metrics for economies are only reported when there are 100 or more unique developers performing the relevant activity within the time period (datasheet l.25 and l.120)
definitions.location: assigned by the developer's IP address, the mode of daily samples in the quarter (datasheet l.27)

params.excludeReason: EU is an aggregate reported beside its member states (DATASETS.md B6); counting it would count those developers twice.

scenes.chartTitle: Developers who pushed to TypeScript and JavaScript repositories
scenes.alt: Line chart of developers pushing to TypeScript and to JavaScript repositories each quarter, summed over the {fig:panel_economies} economies reported for both languages in every quarter from {fig:first_quarter} to {fig:last_quarter}.
scenes.narration: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub? Every quarter, GitHub counts the developers in each economy who push code to repositories in each language. We followed the {fig:panel_economies} economies reported for both languages in every quarter, from {fig:first_quarter} to {fig:last_quarter}.

scenes.chartTitle: TypeScript pushers as a share of JavaScript pushers
scenes.alt: Line chart of TypeScript pushers as a percentage of JavaScript pushers, rising from {fig:ratio_first_pct} in {fig:first_quarter} to {fig:ratio_last_pct} in {fig:last_quarter}.
scenes.narration: Relative to JavaScript, yes, and quickly. In {fig:first_quarter}, TypeScript had {fig:ratio_first_pct} as many pushers as JavaScript. By {fig:last_quarter}, it had {fig:ratio_last_pct}. In raw numbers, though, JavaScript's lead grew, from {fig:gap_first_millions} to {fig:gap_last_millions} pushers, because both languages grew.

scenes.chartTitle: How many times over each language's pushers grew
scenes.alt: Bar chart of the growth multiple of pushers for the {fig:top_n} languages with the most pushers in {fig:last_quarter}; {fig:fastest_top_language} grew fastest, {fig:a_growth_x} over.
scenes.narration: Over those {fig:span_years} years, TypeScript pushers grew {fig:a_growth_x} over, and JavaScript pushers {fig:b_growth_x}. Among the {fig:top_n} languages with the most pushers, the fastest growing was {fig:fastest_top_language}.

scenes.chartTitle: Year-on-year change in the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio
scenes.alt: Bar chart of the yearly change in the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio; the last year's rise of {fig:ratio_gain_last_pts} is the largest, against at most {fig:ratio_gain_max_earlier_pts} in earlier years.
scenes.narration: The ratio moved fastest in the last year: it rose {fig:ratio_gain_last_pts}, against at most {fig:ratio_gain_max_earlier_pts} in any earlier year.

scenes.chartTitle: The TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio, economy by economy
scenes.alt: Histogram of the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio across the {fig:panel_economies} economies in {fig:first_quarter} and in {fig:last_quarter}; {fig:econ_at_threshold_last} economies are at {fig:threshold_pct} or more in the later quarter.
scenes.narration: Economy by economy, the picture is the same. TypeScript reached {fig:threshold_pct} of JavaScript's pushers in {fig:econ_at_threshold_last} of the {fig:panel_economies} economies, up from {fig:econ_at_threshold_first} in {fig:first_year}. The highest ratio was {fig:max_ratio_last_pct}.

scenes.alt: Line chart of how many economies GitHub reports each quarter for TypeScript and for JavaScript; for TypeScript it rose from {fig:econ_reported_a_first} to {fig:econ_reported_a_last}.
scenes.narration: Some limits. GitHub leaves out economies with too few active developers; for TypeScript, the number reported rose from {fig:econ_reported_a_first} to {fig:econ_reported_a_last}, which is why we followed a fixed set. Only public repositories count, a developer who pushes in both languages counts under each, and location comes from IP addresses. The data shows how many developers pushed, not why. The data is GitHub's Innovation Graph, dedicated to the public domain.
